summary: Specifies DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that configure hosts with the addresses of Port Control Protocol servers.

eli5.summary: A computer joining a network needs to know where the port-opening helper lives. These options tell it automatically.

questions: how do clients find a pcp server
what is the dhcpv6 pcp server option
how does a pcp client find a pcp server
subtitle: How a DHCP server can tell a host where its Port Control Protocol server lives, over both IPv4 and IPv6.

tldr.problem: A host that wants to use the Port Control Protocol (PCP) needs the IP address of a PCP server, and nothing in DHCP could deliver that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines one DHCPv6 option (OPTION_V6_PCP_SERVER, code 86) and one DHCPv4 option (OPTION_V4_PCP_SERVER, code 158) that carry lists of PCP server addresses, where each list stands for one distinct PCP server.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can learn their PCP servers automatically. The grouping of addresses into lists tells the client whether to talk to several servers or just pick one address.

today: RFC 7291 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on PCP as defined in RFC 6887.

sections.title: What the Options Are For
sections.content:
This RFC defines options for DHCPv4 (RFC 2131) and DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) that configure a host with the IP addresses of a PCP server. PCP itself is defined in RFC 6887. A PCP server is the element that receives and processes PCP requests, and it may be separate from the NAT or firewall it controls.

A PCP server may be reachable at several IP addresses, so the option carries a list of addresses. The option can also carry several lists. That grouping is a hint to the PCP client: it needs to know whether to create entries on all the PCP servers (for example with multi-homing, or several PCP-controlled devices that provide different services) or to use just one address from the list (for example a redundancy group or a proxy-based model).
sections.eli5: A network can hand your computer a short list of helpers to ask. Sometimes you must ask every helper on the list, and sometimes any one of them will do.

sections.title: The DHCPv6 PCP Server Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 option has an Option-code of OPTION_V6_PCP_SERVER (86), an Option-length and then one or more IPv6 addresses. The length counts the address field in octets and MUST be a multiple of 16. IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses are allowed, and a client that receives one reads it as meaning the PCP server has that IPv4 address.

To return more than one PCP server, as opposed to more than one address for a single server, the DHCPv6 server sends several instances of the option. The client MUST be ready to receive several instances and treats each as a separate PCP server.

To ask for the option, the client lists OPTION_V6_PCP_SERVER in an Option Request Option. The client MUST silently discard multicast and host loopback addresses in the option.
sections.eli5: On IPv6 the network sends one note per helper. Each note holds one or more addresses for that helper, and a computer ignores addresses that cannot possibly be a real helper.

sections.title: The DHCPv4 PCP Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 option has a Code of OPTION_V4_PCP_SERVER (158) and a Length with a minimum of 5. After that come one or more lists, each made of a List-Length byte (which MUST be a multiple of 4) followed by that many bytes of IPv4 addresses.

Here the several servers are packed inside a single option, so each list is treated as a separate PCP server. Because a DHCPv4 option is limited to 255 octets, an option that grows beyond that MUST use the long-option mechanism of RFC 3396.

The client asks for the option in a Parameter Request List option (RFC 2132), MUST be ready to receive several lists, and MUST silently discard multicast and host loopback addresses.
sections.eli5: On IPv4 all the helpers go on one big note. Each helper gets its own short list, and each list starts with a number telling how long it is.

sections.title: Rules for DHCP Servers
sections.content:
If an administrator configures several addresses, the DHCP server MUST be told explicitly whether they belong to the same PCP server or to distinct ones. Same server means they go in one instance (or one list) of the option. Distinct servers means one list per server.

Two things are forbidden. A DHCP server MUST NOT merge the addresses of several PCP servers into one list, and MUST NOT split the addresses of one server into several lists. The RFC gives an example: when a name resolves to several addresses, they all belong together and go into a single block.

DHCPv6 servers that fill the option by looking up names need a way to say whether to query for A records or only AAAA records. Addresses from A records are returned as IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. The stated reason is deployments where an IPv4-only PCP server is used while only DHCPv6 is available, such as Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333).
sections.eli5: The person running the network must say which addresses are the same helper and which are different helpers. The server must never mix them up.

sections.title: Dual-Stack Hosts and Several Interfaces
sections.content:
A dual-stack host may get a PCP server option over both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6. This RFC does not say how to combine them and points to the work in progress on PCP server selection.

A host may also have several network interfaces, such as 3G and IEEE 802.11, each configured differently. Each PCP server a host learns MUST be associated with the interface it was learned on.
sections.eli5: If your device is on two networks at once, it must remember which network told it about which helper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The section is short. It says the security considerations of RFC 2131 and RFC 3315 apply, and that PCP security is discussed in RFC 6887.

The option is stated to be applicable under the simple threat model of RFC 6887. Whether it is appropriate under the advanced threat model is left open, and the analysis is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The note from the network is only as trustworthy as the network itself. This RFC says it is meant for simple situations and leaves the harder cases for someone else to study.
